title: Photographers of the West
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, critics treated the early photographers of the American West as mere documentarians, their images valued for what they recorded rather than for how they were composed. The assumption was that a camera, unlike a brush, could only copy what stood before it.

That assumption has not survived scrutiny. Surviving correspondence shows that these photographers hauled glass plates and chemicals across mountains in order to reach particular vantage points, waited days for the right light, and sometimes rearranged elements of a scene. Whether such choices amount to artistry remains disputed, but it is no longer plausible to call the pictures neutral records.
